clue.text: 15 of 9 taking a mad gamble, caught withholding

parts.note: taken as written, the first part of the fodder

indicators.note: something mad is crazed and disordered, so the two words beside it are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, the rest of the fodder
read as two words, with + holding: the short word with holds the next letter inside it
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A character in a novel risks everything on a wild bet and is caught concealing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is CHARACTER and 9 is DICKENS, so the definition is a Dickens character. Withholding has to be split as with + holding: WIT(C)H.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel Magwitch is the escaped convict who becomes Pip's secret benefactor in Great Expectations, a novel by Dickens.

clue.text: Quail migrating on the north wind

indicators.note: birds migrating move from place to place, so the bird's letters move around too

parts.note: the game bird, taken letter for letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Quail flying south for winter, carried along by a cold northerly.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquilon is a poetic name, from Latin Aquilo, for the cold wind blowing from the north.

clue.text: Symbolic catechists abandon lying for greed

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so those letters are dropped from the word for untruthfulness

parts.note: mendacity is the habit of lying
in the Prayer Book catechism the answer to 'What is your name?' is 'N. or M.', letters standing for any name

explanation.surface: Teachers of religion give up telling lies, only to fall into the sin of gluttony.
explanation.walkthrough: The Book of Common Prayer catechism opens 'What is your Name? Answer: N. or M.', so the catechists' symbols are M and N; drop both from MENDACITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Edacity is a rare, learned word for voracity or gluttony, a hunger that easily stands in for greed.

clue.text: Homer going West on 15 March?

parts.note: Mae West, the American film actress
taken as written
the Ides of March fall on 15 March in the Roman calendar

explanation.surface: A man called Homer dying, or heading west, on the Ides of March like Caesar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going West' suggests dying, but West is the actress Mae West; and here 15 is a plain date, not the cross-reference it is elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Maeonides, 'the Maeonian', is a classical epithet for the poet Homer, supposedly born in Maeonia in Lydia.

clue.text: He proved his logic in the Okavango Delta

indicators.note: the name sits in the place-name that follows, running across its two words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone demonstrated their reasoning out in the swamps of Botswana's Okavango Delta.
explanation.walkthrough: The accent on Gödel is dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Kurt Gödel was the logician whose incompleteness theorems proved deep limits of formal logical systems.

clue.text: One sergeant with two names: you say he''s John Doe

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
a sergeant is a non-commissioned officer
N is the abbreviation for name, twice

indicators.note: 'you say' asks for the letter whose spoken name matches the pronoun

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced like the pronoun

explanation.surface: A soldier with an alias tells you he is an unidentified man.
explanation.definitionFit: Inconnu is French for an unknown person, and John Doe is the placeholder name for an unidentified man.

clue.text: Around Grozny there's no size for type of skullcap

indicators.note: 'there's no' means the measure that follows is missing from the region's name

parts.note: Chechnia, a variant spelling of Chechnya, is the republic whose capital is Grozny
an en is a printer's measure, a size used for type

explanation.surface: In the region round Grozny you cannot get a skullcap in your size.
explanation.walkthrough: Chechnia is an accepted spelling of Chechnya; removing the en, written N, leaves the cap.
explanation.definitionFit: A chechia is a close-fitting cylindrical woollen cap worn in North Africa, a kind of skullcap.

clue.text: Nothing in getting a mug shot of this 15 of 9

indicators.note: the symbol for nothing goes in among the following words before they are mixed
something shot is ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter
O is the figure zero

explanation.surface: Coming away empty-handed from getting a police photograph taken of this rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 of 9 is a character of Dickens; a mug shot fits a swindler, which is the joke of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Montague Tigg is the confidence trickster in Martin Chuzzlewit who runs a fraudulent insurance company.

clue.text: Lay spoken of solvers no longer with us

indicators.note: spoken means the phrase that follows is heard rather than read

parts.words: of solvers no longer with us
parts.note: solvers are 'you' to the setter, and those no longer with us are 'late'

explanation.surface: An obituary-like remark about departed puzzle solvers, delivered as a secular hymn or lay.
explanation.walkthrough: Lay looks like a poem or a layman; here it is the verb, as a hen lays.
explanation.definitionFit: To ovulate is to release an egg from the ovary, which is what laying means in a biological sense.

clue.text: Writer's devil …

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Charles, the Victorian novelist

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue, which uses devil a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of a famous English novelist is also a mild oath standing in for the devil.

clue.text: 15 of 9 used 15 23 for 15 22

parts.note: surface reading: a cross-referencing puzzle putting one entry in place of another
setter's reading: character 23 means the 23rd letter of the alphabet, W, and 15 22 is the 22nd, V

explanation.walkthrough: 15 is CHARACTER and 9 is DICKENS; 'character 23 for character 22' is W for V, the famous Cockney trait of this servant, who says 'wery' for 'very'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sam Weller is Mr Pickwick's witty cockney manservant in The Pickwick Papers, a novel by Dickens.

clue.text: … not like another writer

indicators.note: the dots carry over 'devil' from the previous clue, and to devil is to mangle or tear up

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Read with the previous clue, one author's devilry is unlike that of another writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 9 and 11 together: 'Writer's devil ... not like another writer'; devil does double duty as the anagram signal for the letters of 'not like'.
explanation.definitionFit: J. R. R. Tolkien, author of The Lord of the Rings, is a second author following on from Dickens.

clue.text: Arkwright's lad succeeding one archbishop, then another

parts.note: Cosmo Lang was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1928 to 1942
an ark-wright is an ark builder, Noah, whose son was Ham

explanation.surface: Arkwright's young assistant, as in Open All Hours, takes over from one church leader and then a second.
explanation.walkthrough: Arkwright looks like the inventor Richard Arkwright or the shopkeeper of the BBC sitcom Open All Hours; split it as ark + wright, a builder of the Ark. 'Succeeding' puts the son after the archbishop.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Langham was Archbishop of Canterbury in the 1360s, so he is a further holder of that office.

clue.text: US city reporter switching material to get the sack

indicators.note: switching swaps the two parts round, so the first moves to the end

parts.note: New York
a gun makes a report when fired

explanation.surface: A journalist in an American city changes fabrics and is promptly fired.
explanation.walkthrough: Reporter is not a journalist here but something that makes a report, a bang.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunny is the coarse jute cloth that sacks and bags are made from, so it is the stuff of sacking.

clue.text: Art of French Revolution period?

parts.note: de is French for of
a coup is a sudden overthrow of government
an age is an era or period

explanation.surface: A question about the painting and sculpture of the era of the French Revolution.
explanation.definitionFit: Decoupage is the decorative craft of covering objects with cut-out paper designs and varnish.

clue.text: Eccentric type

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an odd, colourful person
second meaning: a printed letter or symbol

explanation.walkthrough: Eccentric reads as an adjective on type, but it is the noun, an eccentric.
explanation.definitionFit: A quirky individual is called a real character, and each printed letter or symbol is also a character.

clue.text: Fits city lights one after another

parts.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London
lamps are lights
one is I, then another one is A

explanation.surface: Street lamps in a city come on in sequence, maybe triggering seizures.
explanation.walkthrough: Fits looks like a verb; it is the plural noun, seizures.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclampsia is a condition of pregnancy marked by convulsions, so it is a matter of seizures.

clue.text: Constant brightness measured here

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Constant, first name of the English composer and conductor
second meaning: a unit of luminance

explanation.walkthrough: Constant looks like an adjective describing the brightness, but it is a first name: Constant Lambert wrote The Rio Grande.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer Constant Lambert shares his surname with the old unit used for measuring the luminance of a surface.

clue.text: Invasive 15 of Welles out of Wells

definitions.text: Invasive 15 of Welles out of Wells

parts.note: surface reading: an intrusive figure who escaped from some wells
setter's reading: an invader in Orson Welles's radio drama taken from H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds

explanation.walkthrough: 15 is CHARACTER; Orson Welles's 1938 broadcast of H. G. Wells's novel panicked listeners with an invasion from the red planet.
explanation.definitionFit: The invaders in The War of the Worlds come from Mars, and Welles dramatised them on radio.

clue.text: Here on earth or under it?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: 'here ...', in this mortal world

explanation.walkthrough: The old phrase 'here below' means on earth rather than in heaven, while plainly below is under the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes life in this world in the phrase 'here below', and also means beneath something.

clue.text: Wellington's part to play in probibition busting

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a wellington is a rubber boot, and this is its shaft, the part round the leg
second meaning: illicit liquor trade that defied the American alcohol ban

explanation.surface: The Duke of Wellington's role in some campaign to break a ban.
explanation.walkthrough: A wellington is a British rubber boot, named after the Duke, not the man himself; 'probibition' is the source's typo for prohibition.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper shaft of a boot is called its leg, and bootlegging was smuggling illicit liquor during the 1920s American ban on alcohol.

clue.text: They sack the string players, you say?

indicators.note: 'you say' means the players' title is heard, not spelt

parts.note: lutenists, players of the lute, a stringed instrument

explanation.surface: An orchestra manager dismisses the violinists and cellists.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack looks like dismissing staff; it means plunder.
explanation.definitionFit: Plunderers who sack a town are people who steal goods during disorder.

clue.text: I'm right! "Smee", alternatively, is "Duck"

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: alternatively suggests another version, so the name and letter are set in a different order

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
Captain Hook's boatswain in Peter Pan, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Captain Hook's pirate Smee insists he is right, or is simply a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck someone is to plunge them briefly under water, which is to submerge them.

clue.text: Old comedian bearing lines from Bunthorne with polish

parts.note: E is the compass bearing east
Bunthorne is the setter, who would call himself me
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a set of lines

explanation.surface: A vintage comic delivers the setter's jokes, smoothly polished.
explanation.walkthrough: From means following, so the lines come after the setter's me. Dick Emery was a British TV comedian of the 1960s and 70s.
explanation.definitionFit: Emery is the abrasive powder used to polish metal, and Dick Emery was a well-known British comic.

clue.text: Nothing much left after chopper chopped salamander

indicators.note: a chopped tool has lost its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: an axe is a chopper
O is the figure zero
a lot is much
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: After an axe has been at it, little of the poor salamander remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the shortened chopper in front of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The axolotl is a Mexican salamander that keeps its larval gills into adult life.

clue.text: Ape Athens gave initially to Ceres, I gathered

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of the verb before it is used

parts.note: the first letter of gave

indicators.note: things gathered are collected up together in no fixed order, so the goddess and pronoun are rearranged

parts.note: the Roman goddess and the pronoun, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: An imitator of Athens offered tribute to the Roman corn goddess Ceres, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: Ape is the verb, to imitate; to Grecise is to make or become Greek in style.
explanation.definitionFit: Grecise means to imitate Greek ways, and Athens stands for Greek culture, so aping Athens is Grecising.

clue.text: This offensive little unit, essentially nitro, explodes: it blows their heads off!

definitions.text: This offensive little unit, essentially nitro, explodes: it blows their heads off!

indicators.note: the heads of the words are their first letters, which are all that is kept

parts.words: This offensive little unit, essentially nitro, explodes
parts.note: the first letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: A warning about a small military explosive device that decapitates its victims.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: toluene, nitrated, becomes trinitrotoluene, TNT, the high explosive.
explanation.definitionFit: Toluene is the hydrocarbon at the heart of TNT, the nitro explosive that blows things apart.

clue.text: 9 15: good chap! Fair of Delius to enter "Yes! No Bananas"

parts.note: a saint, abbreviated St, is a good person

indicators.note: the musical title goes to enter, or go inside, the mixed-up words
bananas is slang for crazy, so the two quoted words are scrambled

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter
Brigg Fair is an orchestral rhapsody by Frederick Delius

explanation.surface: Delius's music is introduced into the old song 'Yes! We Have No Bananas', a nice fellow says.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 15 is a Dickens character; Brigg Fair is named after a Lincolnshire town's fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Briggs, nicknamed Stoney, is one of the boys at Doctor Blimber's school in Dickens's Dombey and Son.
